title: Drawing a drawdown
objectives: Build the wealth curve with cumprod and plot its running peak
Draw the drawdown as a filled area below zero and annotate the maximum drawdown
Choose a log axis so a long history does not exaggerate late falls

screens.title: New highs
screens.prose: A fund's price over twelve days. An investor's pain is measured from the best price seen so far, so we start by finding the highs.

screens.title: Drawdown
screens.prose: The fall below the running peak $M_t = \max_{s \le t} P_s$ is the **drawdown**: $D_t = \dfrac{P_t}{M_t} - 1$. It is 0 at a new high and negative below one.
screens.question: Work out $D_8$, the drawdown on day 8, in %.

hints.text: Which two prices does the drawdown compare?
The running peak on day 8 is day 5's £112.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the day 8 close by the running peak, then subtract 1.

byKey.pounds: You entered the £12.32 gap as a percentage. Divide it by the £112.00 peak first.
byKey.sign: The price is below its peak, so the drawdown is negative.
byKey.trough: You divided by £99.68. Measure from the peak, £112.00.
byKey.yesterday: You measured from day 7's close. A drawdown is measured from the running peak.

explain.text: Dividing by the running peak gives $\tfrac{99.68}{112.00} = 0.89$, so the drawdown is −11%. The most negative $D_t$ over the whole history is the **maximum drawdown**.

screens.title: From returns to wealth
screens.prose: Often we hold returns, not prices. A strategy makes +50%, −50%, +50%, −50% on four days. Wealth grows by multiplying: $W_t = (1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)\cdots(1 + r_t)$, which is `np.cumprod(1 + rets)`.

state.caption: Wealth of £1: drawn after you answer

Each day multiplies wealth by $1 + r$: 1.5, then 0.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £1 by $1 + r$ for each day in turn.

byKey.added: You added the returns: +50 − 50 + 50 − 50 = 0. A 50% loss on £1.50 takes away £0.75, not £0.50.
byKey.product: You multiplied the returns themselves. Multiply $1 + r$ instead: 1.5 and 0.5.
byKey.two-days: That is the wealth after two days. Carry on for days 3 and 4.

explain.text: Each day multiplies wealth by $1 + r$, so £1 becomes £1.50, £0.75, £1.125 and £0.5625. Adding the returns, the dashed line, says nothing was lost. `np.cumprod(1 + rets)` builds the solid line, and its drawdown is what we chart.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def plot_drawdown(prices):
    prices = np.array(prices, dtype=float)
    days = np.arange(1, len(prices) + 1)
    peak = np.maximum.accumulate(prices)
    dd = prices / peak - 1
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.fill_between(days, dd, 0, color="tab:red", alpha=0.4)
    return ax

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def plot_drawdown(prices):
    prices = np.array(prices, dtype=float)
    days = np.arange(1, len(prices) + 1)
    peak = np.maximum.accumulate(prices)
    dd = prices / peak - 1
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.fill_between(days, dd, 0, color="tab:red", alpha=0.4)
    i = np.argmin(dd)
    ax.annotate(f"{dd[i]:.1%}", xy=(days[i], dd[i]), xytext=(days[i] + 1, dd[i] - 0.03),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
    return ax

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
The drawdown chart in four lines:

```python
wealth = np.cumprod(1 + rets)
peak = np.maximum.accumulate(wealth)
dd = wealth / peak - 1
ax.fill_between(days, dd, 0, alpha=0.4)
```

That is $D_t = \dfrac{W_t}{\max_{s \le t} W_s} - 1$, always 0 or below.

That finds the first time the highest peak is reached, not the trough after it.
`min` gives the value, −0.11, not its position. `argmin` gives the position.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def drawdown_figure(rets):
    rets = np.asarray(rets, dtype=float)
    days = np.arange(1, len(rets) + 1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
    wealth = np.cumprod(1 + rets)
    peak = np.maximum.accumulate(wealth)
    dd = wealth / peak - 1
    axes[0].plot(days, wealth)
    axes[0].plot(days, peak, linestyle="--")
    axes[1].fill_between(days, dd, 0, alpha=0.4)
    i = np.argmin(dd)
    axes[1].annotate(f"{dd[i]:.1%}", xy=(days[i], dd[i]), xytext=(days[i] + 1, dd[i] - 0.02),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
    return fig, axes

ideas: The running peak, `np.maximum.accumulate`, is the best price so far; the drawdown is the price over that peak, minus 1.
Draw the drawdown with `ax.fill_between(days, dd, 0)` and mark the trough with `ax.annotate` at `np.argmin(dd)`.
From returns, build wealth with `np.cumprod(1 + rets)`; on a long history a log axis keeps late falls honest.

formula.name: Drawdown
formula.note: Maximum drawdown is the most negative D_t.

quiz.prose: A strategy returns +10% one day and −10% the next. A colleague builds the wealth curve with `1 + np.cumsum(rets)`.
quiz.question: What does £1 really end at, and what does the colleague's curve show?

options.why: You added the returns too. −10% of £1.10 is £0.11, not £0.10.
You swapped them. The sum gives £1.00; compounding gives £0.99.
The loss is taken from a bigger amount, £1.10, so wealth ends lower, not higher.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by $1 + r$ each day.

explain.text: Compounding gives $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$. Adding gives $1 + 0.1 - 0.1 = 1$, which hides the loss and so hides part of the drawdown.

quiz.prose: An index went from £100 to £3,000 over 40 years. An early crash of 30% looks like a ripple on a linear chart beside a recent 10% dip.
quiz.question: Which change makes equal % falls look the same size?

options.why: That is still a linear axis. A £ move still looks bigger when the price is higher.
That relabels the ticks; it does not change where the line is drawn.
That adds a panel with a shared x axis. The price panel would still be linear.

feedback.correct: On a log axis equal ratios take equal heights.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which option changes how heights are drawn?

explain.text: A log axis spaces 100, 200 and 400 equally, so every 50% fall has the same height. The early 30% crash then looks three times the depth of the 10% dip.

quiz.question: What does the chart show?

options.text: An area above zero, in £, that is larger when prices are higher

options.why: It is flipped and also in £. A £10 gap at £200 is a 5% drawdown; at £50 it is 20%.
It shades between any two curves, above or below zero.
There is no division by the peak, so the numbers are £ gaps, not percentages.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the sign and the units of `peak - prices`.

explain.text: `peak - prices` is a £ gap, never negative, so the area sits above zero. It also inflates falls at higher prices, the same trap as a linear axis. Divide by the peak: `prices / peak - 1`.
